title: A data-driven approach with explainable artificial intelligence for customer churn prediction in the telecommunications industry
harvard_reference: Asif, D., Arif, M.S. and Mukheimer, A. (2025) 'A data-driven approach with explainable artificial intelligence for customer churn prediction in the telecommunications industry', Results in Engineering, 26, 104629. doi:10.1016/j.rineng.2025.104629.
abstract_summary: Proposes XAI-Churn TriBoost, a soft-voting ensemble of XGBoost, CatBoost and LightGBM (weights 2:1:3) for telecom churn prediction. The data are NOT the IBM/Kaggle Telco file: the paper uses train.csv from the Expresso Churn Prediction Challenge on Zindi (Senegalese prepaid operator), 2,154,048 records and 17 stated variables, with churn defined as the customer becoming inactive with no transactions for 90 consecutive days; 19% of records are churners. Preprocessing: drop zone1/zone2 (>90% missing), MRG (one value), user_id, region (dropped 'to avoid introducing location-based bias' and to generalise across countries), top_pack and freq_top_pack (140 categories); ordinal encoding; iterative imputation with a Bayesian ridge estimator (median initialisation, converged after 15 iterations); sequential robust -> standard -> min-max scaling; a new feature off_net = tigo + orange; Boruta with random forest (100 trees, percentile 90, alpha 0.05) leaving nine features (montant, frequence_rech, revenue, arpu_segment, frequence, data_volume, on_net, regularity, off_net). Stratified 60/40 split (random_state 42); SMOTE applied to the training set only with k=5 and sampling_strategy 0.5, raising the minority share from 19% to 33% (1,575,055 training rows; 861,620 test rows). Hyperparameters tuned by RandomizedSearchCV. Reported test results: accuracy 0.9644, precision 0.9282, recall 0.8782, F1 0.9025, AUC-ROC 0.9828, PR-AUC 0.9601. Table 9 baselines (same preprocessing): decision tree 0.9395 acc / 0.8468 F1; logistic regression 0.8200 / 0.6338; Gaussian NB 0.5682 / 0.4565 (recall 0.9672); Bernoulli NB 0.7952 / 0.5519; ridge classifier 0.8011 / 0.6164; SGD 0.7993 / 0.6146. A 27-combination ablation of ensemble weights (Table 8) spans only accuracy 0.9635-0.9644 and F1 0.8999-0.9025. LIME gives local explanations for a 53%-churn and a 78%-no-churn instance (revenue, regularity, arpu_segment); SHAP force/waterfall plots (regularity +0.21, revenue +0.06, arpu_segment -0.03), a beeswarm plot and a mean-|SHAP| ranking identify regularity (number of activities over the last three months) and montant (top-up amount) as the top drivers, followed by arpu_segment and revenue. Future work only: multi-industry datasets, a web app with real-time monitoring, a feedback loop and periodic retraining.

claims_supported.claim: Tree ensembles (random forest / gradient boosting) achieve top or near-top ROC-AUC on telecom churn data, often close to logistic regression.
claims_supported.where: Partly contradicted. The boosting ensemble is the top model on accuracy, precision and F1 (Section 5, Table 9: TriBoost 0.9644 / 0.9282 / 0.8782 / 0.9025) and Section 4.2.5 / Fig. 10 report AUC-ROC 0.9828 and PR-AUC 0.9601 for the ensemble, but no ROC-AUC is reported for ANY baseline, so the paper contains no ROC-AUC comparison at all. Random forest is not evaluated as a classifier (it is only the base learner inside Boruta feature selection). The 'close to logistic regression' half is directly contradicted on this dataset: logistic regression scores accuracy 0.8200, precision 0.5125, recall 0.8304, F1 0.6338 (Table 9), i.e. about 14 accuracy points and 27 F1 points below the ensemble, and even a single decision tree (0.9395 / 0.8468) beats it by a wide margin. Note this is the 2.15-million-row Expresso prepaid usage dataset, not the IBM Telco data on which the near-parity pattern is usually reported, so this paper is evidence AGAINST parity on large usage-count data, not for it.

claims_supported.claim: Explainability (SHAP or similar) identifies contract type, tenure and monthly charges (or equivalent) as key churn drivers.
claims_supported.where: Not supported as phrased. SHAP mean-|SHAP| ranking (Section 4.4, Fig. 16), the Discussion and the Conclusion name 'regularity' (number of activities over the last three months) and 'montant' (top-up amount) as the most important features, followed by 'arpu_segment' and 'revenue'; the abstract states 'Key factors impacting churn include regularity and montant'. The dataset is prepaid and has no contract-type variable at all. No tenure variable appears in the final feature set (Table 2). The Zindi source data does contain a TENURE column (subscription duration band; confirmed from a third-party data dictionary of the Expresso challenge, not from the paper), and the paper's own counts - 11 features retained after cleaning (Section 3.2.1), 10 after merging tigo+orange, 9 after Boruta (Section 5) - imply that the single feature Boruta eliminated was tenure, although the paper never names it. The only loose 'equivalent' is that spend features (montant, revenue, arpu_segment) play the role monthly charges play in the IBM Telco data. Also note the paper says (Section 4.4, beeswarm) that HIGH regularity pushes predictions toward churn, which is counter-intuitive and should be checked against Fig. 15 before being cited.

claims_supported.claim: Business or profit-oriented evaluation changes which model or threshold is preferred compared with accuracy-only evaluation.
claims_supported.where: Not addressed. Section 4.2 defines the evaluation as accuracy, precision, recall, F1, AUC-ROC and PR-AUC only; there is no cost matrix, profit measure, expected-value analysis, uplift or threshold optimisation anywhere in the paper. The default 0.5 decision rule is implied (the LIME example with 53% churn probability is classed as churn, Section 4.3.1). Ensemble weights were chosen in the ablation (Table 8) by accuracy/F1. The Discussion's statement that the ensemble is 'the most reliable and practical choice for businesses focused on customer retention strategies' is argued from precision and F1, not from any business metric.

claims_supported.claim: Any other specific finding this paper makes that would be useful for a critical discussion of churn prediction methods, imbalance handling, calibration, uplift, survival, fairness or deployment (state it precisely).
claims_supported.where: (a) Imbalance handling (Section 3.6): SMOTE is applied to the training set only, with an explicit statement that resampling the whole dataset 'would alter the real-world distribution', and only PARTIAL rebalancing is used (sampling_strategy 0.5: minority share 19% -> 33%, not 1:1). (b) Ensemble weighting adds almost nothing measurable: across all 27 weight combinations in Table 8 accuracy ranges 0.9635-0.9644 and F1 0.8999-0.9025, differences at the third or fourth decimal with no confidence intervals or repeated runs; evaluation is a single 60/40 hold-out (Section 3.5), with cross-validation used only inside RandomizedSearchCV (folds not stated). (c) Linear models cluster together (LR 0.8200, ridge 0.8011, SGD 0.7993 accuracy; F1 0.61-0.63) while a single decision tree reaches 0.9395, indicating strong non-linearity in prepaid usage-count features after the authors' scaling pipeline (Table 9). (d) Gaussian naive Bayes illustrates the recall/precision trade-off: recall 0.9672 but precision 0.2988 and accuracy 0.5682 (Table 9, Section 5). (e) Missing data: iterative imputation with Bayesian ridge (median initialisation, tolerance 1e-5, converged after 15 of 20 iterations) rather than deletion or mean fill, because some columns exceed 50% missing (Section 3.2.3). (f) Feature selection by Boruta with a random-forest base (Table 1) is presented as a bias-reducing alternative to threshold- or domain-driven manual selection (Section 3.4). (g) Fairness/generalisability gesture only: the region feature is dropped 'to avoid introducing location-based bias' and to keep the model applicable across countries (Section 3.2.1); there is no formal fairness, calibration, uplift or survival analysis. (h) Deployment is future work only: a web application with real-time data links, monitoring, customer segmentation, a user feedback loop and periodic retraining to cope with drift such as 'economic turmoil or changes in the market' (Sections 5-6). (i) Compute: the whole pipeline on 2.15 million rows ran on a single HP ZBook laptop (i9-9880H, Quadro T2000, 32 GB RAM) (Section 4.1.2). (j) The authors themselves position IBM-Telco-scale studies (7,043 samples, 20 features) as small-data contrasts (Section 5, Table 10).

caveats: 1) Dataset mismatch: this is the Expresso (Zindi, Senegal, prepaid) dataset with 2.15 million rows and nine usage/spend features, not the IBM/Kaggle Telco file; there is no contract, tenure, payment-method or monthly-charges variable in the model, so its feature-importance findings do not transfer to a Telco report and its 0.96 accuracy / 0.98 AUC must not be compared with the ~0.80 accuracy / ~0.84 AUC typical of Telco studies. 2) The paper reports no AUC for any baseline and never evaluates random forest as a classifier, so it cannot support statements about ensemble versus logistic-regression ROC-AUC. 3) Logistic regression is run on heavy-tailed count features after ordinal encoding and a robust/standard/min-max scaling chain with no interaction or log terms, so its weak result is partly a specification artefact. 4) Single 60/40 hold-out, no confidence intervals, no repeated seeds; the ablation shows weight choices differ only at the third or fourth decimal, so the claimed superiority of the 2:1:3 weighting is not meaningful. 5) SMOTE is partial (to 33% minority) and applied after scaling; no comparison with class weights or no-resampling is given, so the paper cannot show that SMOTE helped. 6) Accuracy is inflated by the 81% non-churn base rate; the PR-AUC of 0.9601 and F1 of 0.9025 are the more informative figures. 7) Section 4.4 states that high 'regularity' values push predictions toward churn, the opposite of the intuitive direction (and of what Zindi community analyses report: low activity -> churn); the paper does not reconcile this, so cite the ranking, not the direction, unless Fig. 15 is checked. 8) Internal inconsistencies: Highlights give precision 92.80% and F1 90.24% while the abstract and Table 8 give 92.82% and 90.25%; Section 5 text credits reference [47] (7,043 samples) with 0.981 accuracy but Table 10 lists [47] at 0.79 accuracy / 0.84 AUC; the '1.58 million' training records quoted in the Conclusion is the post-SMOTE count (original training set 1,292,428); the feature 'arpu_segment' is misspelt 'apru_segment' in Table 4 and Section 4.4. 9) No calibration, uplift, survival, cost-sensitive or fairness analysis; deployment is described only as future work. 10) The venue is a broad-scope, APC-funded Elsevier mega-journal (single-anonymous review); treat it as legitimate but give its methodological claims less weight than a specialist journal would carry.
